headline: OEMpocalypse: Unprivileged Android app roots Samsung, Xiaomi, and others with a single strategy
summary: A new series details a single strategy to gain root access on Samsung, Xiaomi, and Oppo/OnePlus/Realme devices from an unprivileged Android app. This method targets OEM-specific kernel drivers and sandbox escapes.
details: A new vulnerability series, dubbed "OEMpocalypse," demonstrates how an unprivileged Android app can achieve root access on devices from major OEMs like Samsung, Xiaomi, and Oppo/OnePlus/Realme. This exploit leverages a single, consistent strategy across multiple manufacturers.

The core idea involves targeting code written by Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs). Specifically, it exploits a page Use-After-Free (UAF) bug in an OEM-specific kernel driver, combined with an OEM-specific sandbox escape to reach the driver when required by SELinux policy.

The strategy has been instantiated three times, covering all Samsung flagship devices (Galaxy S23 through S26 series and recent Z series), a large share of Xiaomi mid-range to flagship devices, and recent Oppo, OnePlus, and Realme flagship devices.

An unprivileged Android app typically faces strict security layers: Unix DAC via UID, SELinux as the Mandatory Access Control, and system call filtering via seccomp. These mechanisms severely limit an app's access to the kernel and most of the driver stack.

The research aims for an ideal weaponized exploit that is reliable, portable, and universal. This means it should succeed near-100% regardless of defenses, require minimal adjustments across kernel versions or OEMs, and cover as many devices as possible with a single exploit.
